ipe-18-cross-division-coordination.transcript:
Cross-Division Coordination

Co-host: Welcome. Think about the last time you sent something to another team and thought, that part is finished. Let's follow an example of what happens next. As you listen, consider this question: what does the next person actually need from us?

Host: We are following a disability services team preparing a change to the information providers submit. Policy has written the change, operations has updated its instructions, and communications is preparing a notice. Everyone is busy, and everyone believes their own part is on schedule.

Co-host: Then a county partner calls. Families are asking about a change they cannot find explained clearly. The notice arrived after the change began. A plain-language version was drafted, but a later edit never reached its writer. Several people are looking at different versions.

Host: My first reaction would be to find out why the notice was late. That seems like a straightforward problem. Set a deadline for communications, put it on the calendar, and make sure somebody watches it next time.

Co-host: That could help with timing. But would it catch the missing plain-language version? Or tell the county which version to use? Before we name a person who missed a step, let's trace how the work actually moved.

Host: So we need a little more of the story. Policy sent a final document to operations. Operations sent revised instructions to communications. Language support received an earlier draft. The county received the instructions, but not the explanation families needed.

Co-host: Let's make the choice concrete. The team can add another reminder email, ask county partners to explain everything themselves, or agree on a small package that stays with the change as it moves. Which one would you try first?

Host: I would try the package. A reminder does not tell anyone which draft is current. Asking counties to improvise may create different explanations. But I would keep the package short enough that people actually use it, rather than creating another document nobody opens.

Co-host: Start with the decision and its reason. What is changing, and what problem is it meant to solve? Then include what the next team needs to know about the people affected. Useful context helps them answer a question the original writer did not anticipate.

Host: That does not mean attaching everybody's personal records. For this notice, we need the affected audience, the practical action, and the known communication needs. Any personal information would require its own authorized purpose and appropriate handling. More information is not automatically a better handoff.

Co-host: Then carry the access arrangements. Which versions are needed? Who is preparing them? Where can someone request another format or language? Those questions belong with the change from the beginning, because a finished English document is not necessarily a finished communication.

Host: We also need the clock. There is the team's deadline, but there is also the time a person needs to understand a notice and act. If the two dates leave no usable time between them, a neat calendar will not solve the problem.

Co-host: Finally, name the next contact and who will send the next update. A unit name can be useful, but it is not enough if nobody knows who is watching the question. The person receiving the handoff should confirm what they have accepted.

Host: Here is the complication. The effective date may not be ours to change. We cannot promise families an extension just because our communication was late. How do we act quickly without making a promise another office would have to honor?

Co-host: We separate the immediate communication repair from the decision about dates or individual cases. The team can prepare a corrected explanation and get it through the appropriate review. It also takes the timing problem to the person authorized to decide what remedies are available.

Host: So the county receives a clear update about what is known, what is being checked, and when another answer will arrive. We do not leave them guessing, and we do not turn a possible remedy into a policy announcement before it has been decided.

Co-host: Now let's use the course's handoff map. Picture one row for each change of hands. Write who sends the work, who receives it, what must arrive, what can delay it, and who keeps the affected person informed. Use the order a person experiences.

Host: Our first row is policy to operations. I would add a plain explanation of the purpose, the current approved wording, the effective date, and questions still unresolved. Operations checks that the instructions describe the same change before passing them onward.

Co-host: At the next row, communications and language support need the same current material. The team agrees how later edits will reach everyone preparing a version. A change to one sentence may matter in several formats; it cannot disappear into a single email thread.

Host: For the county handoff, I would include the finished explanation, available formats, a contact for questions, and the date of the next update. Then I would ask a county colleague to describe what they would tell a family. That is more revealing than asking whether they received the email.

Co-host: Suppose that colleague says, I understand what changed, but I still cannot tell someone what to do if the old instructions were already followed. That is a valuable finding. The package arrived, but an important question remained unanswered.

Host: We take that question back before calling the work complete. If the answer needs a program decision, we name who is checking it. Meanwhile, our message says how to get help. Acknowledging an unanswered question can be more useful than sending a confident but incomplete answer.

Co-host: Here is a moment to pause. Think of a handoff in your own work. What do you routinely assume the next person already knows? The reason behind a decision? A promised callback? An accessible version? Choose one assumption you could replace with a direct question.

Host: There is a tradeoff here. Nobody wants every small task to require a meeting. We can scale the effort. A routine request may need a short note. A change affecting many people needs earlier coordination, because fixing the confusion afterward takes much more time.

Co-host: And one person should not become the permanent rescuer of every handoff. In our story, the teams agree who carries each part, who can resolve a disagreement, and how they notice a missing item. Shared responsibility becomes useful when the individual responsibilities are clear.

Host: They try the new arrangement on the next notice. This time a late wording change reaches every writer. The county catches a confusing instruction before release. The notice and its needed versions arrive together, and the question contact knows what has been sent.

Co-host: The handoff is clearer in this example. Sending everything on time is only the first check, though. Did people understand what to do? Did they still have to repeat their questions? Could someone who needed another format find it without an extra search?

Host: The team reviews a small sample of questions and asks partners what remained difficult. It avoids declaring that one successful notice proves the whole process is equitable. It looks for who still met a barrier and makes another specific adjustment.

Co-host: If the map reveals a broader change to a policy or service, the Equity Analysis Toolkit can help you examine who benefits, who carries the burden, what evidence is missing, and which alternatives deserve attention. The map gives that analysis a concrete starting point.

Host: Open Cross-Division Coordination and use its handoff map. Ask your next colleague: what do you need from my step that you usually have to chase? Listen, agree on one change, and check whether it helped. That is a manageable place to begin.

di-accommodations-and-interactive-proces.transcript:
Accommodations and Interactive Problem-Solving

Co-host: Welcome. An important request can arrive in an ordinary sentence: I need the instructions in a different form. Let's consider a conversation about that request, and how a thoughtful first response can make the next step easier.

Host: Consider Jordan, an eligibility specialist. He understands the work, but changes announced only aloud at the morning huddle are hard to use later. He has made two mistakes and has started checking every change with a colleague before acting.

Co-host: Jordan tells his supervisor, Maya, that the difficulty is related to a disability. He asks whether changes could be provided in writing. Maya has another meeting in ten minutes and a busy team. She wants to help, but she is unsure what she can agree to.

Host: I can imagine her saying, of course, just take more notes. It sounds practical. It does not require another person to do anything. But Jordan has already said that the current way information is delivered is not working for him.

Co-host: That response makes him responsible for overcoming the same barrier again. A more useful beginning would be: thank you for telling me. Which part of the huddle is hardest to use afterward, and what kind of written information has helped before?

Host: Does Jordan need to use the words reasonable accommodation? No. Federal employment guidance recognizes requests in ordinary language when a person connects a needed workplace change to a medical condition. The conversation starts with that request; a particular phrase is not the starting signal.

Co-host: Maya does not have to solve the whole situation in ten minutes. She can listen, explain that she will connect with the responsible accommodation contact, and discuss what might help with today's work. A short, useful response is better than a warm response with no next step.

Host: Jordan explains that the difficulty is not understanding the change when he hears it. It is recalling the exact instruction later, especially when several changes arrive together. A short written list, with the date it applies, would help him check his work independently.

Co-host: Now we have a specific barrier and a possible response. We can keep telling Jordan to take notes, ask a coworker to repeat every change, or provide a dependable written summary. Which option best matches what he has described?

Host: The summary seems promising because it provides the information when he needs it. Repeating every change through a coworker might help briefly, but it adds dependence and can introduce a different wording. Still, I would ask Jordan whether a summary really covers the difficulty.

Co-host: He says it would, provided the summary includes last-minute corrections. That detail matters. A document posted before the huddle could look like a solution while missing the very changes he needs. Effective support depends on how the work actually happens.

Host: Maya worries about adding work for the team lead. That is a fair practical question, so they consider how to keep the summary brief. They already send a daily operations message. Could the confirmed changes appear there, with a clear correction when something changes again?

Co-host: They do not decide just by choosing the easiest option for the team. They compare whether the options remove the barrier. Employment guidance allows an effective accommodation to be selected; it does not mean every preferred option must be chosen. Effectiveness remains central to that choice.

Host: And Maya should not treat a busy morning as a final answer about what the organization can provide. She discusses what she can arrange within her authority and brings the formal question to the appropriate human resources or accommodation contact for this workplace.

Co-host: Here is another tempting wrong turn: asking Jordan to explain his diagnosis before discussing the instructions. That could draw the conversation away from the task. Maya already has a useful question to pursue: what information does he need, when does he need it, and in what form?

Host: Sometimes appropriate documentation is needed when disability or the need for accommodation is not apparent. Federal guidance limits that request to relevant information. Maya should use the designated process rather than collecting broad medical history to satisfy her own uncertainty.

Co-host: Let's put the response together. Maya thanks Jordan, confirms the difficulty, and proposes that today's confirmed changes be written down while she contacts the responsible office. She asks whether that will help immediately and agrees when they will check how it worked.

Host: I like that she checks instead of announces. Jordan may know something she has not considered. Perhaps the written message is hard to locate, or the format is difficult to read. Asking about those details treats him as a partner in solving the problem.

Co-host: Jordan and Maya agree to try a short summary in the existing team channel, with the relevant date and a clearly marked correction when needed. That responds to the difficulty Jordan described. Another person or job might need a different solution.

Host: Maya sends the request through the workplace's designated route and tells Jordan who will contact him. She keeps the practical arrangement clear while that conversation continues. She does not tell the team why Jordan asked, because colleagues need the usable instruction, not his private information.

Co-host: Medical information is subject to confidentiality protections and should not be mixed casually into everyday team or performance records. The responsible office can explain appropriate handling. Maya's everyday conversation with the team can stay focused on how confirmed instructions will be shared.

Host: Suppose a colleague asks, why does he get something different? Maya can explain that the team is improving how people access work instructions. She does not need to disclose an accommodation or defend it by describing Jordan's health. Privacy does not prevent a clear explanation of the work.

Co-host: After several days, Jordan says the written summary helps, but corrections are still sometimes mentioned only in passing. The first idea was useful and incomplete. Maya asks the lead to mark corrections in the same place, and they check again after trying that change.

Host: That is a good example of follow-up doing real work. They are not asking whether Jordan is grateful for the adjustment. They are asking whether the information now reaches him in a form he can use. The answer helps them improve the arrangement.

Co-host: The expected accuracy hasn't changed. What changes is how Jordan can get the information he needs to do the work. The written instruction helps him use the same guidance as his colleagues, with less dependence on someone else's memory.

Host: Other colleagues find the written changes useful too. Maya can consider making that a regular practice without announcing whose request prompted it. But a helpful general change does not automatically answer every individual need. She still checks the arrangement with Jordan.

Co-host: Notice where the story has moved. At first, the question seemed to be why Jordan could not keep up with the huddle. Now it is how the team can make important instructions available when people need them. That shift makes a different response possible.

Host: In One DSD, open Accommodations and Interactive Problem-Solving for the conversation sequence and practice questions. Use Find the right person to locate the relevant support route. Check the current contact and process in your workplace rather than relying on a name you remember from years ago.

Co-host: For your next step, identify one work instruction that is easy to miss. Consider whether its format or timing creates an avoidable barrier. If somebody asks for an adjustment, start by understanding the task and what would help, then involve the right person and check the result.

Host: You do not need every answer to respond with care. Listen, ask a useful question, and help the next step happen. A person should leave that first conversation knowing that the barrier was heard and that there is a way forward.

dsd-03-self-direction-independent-living.transcript:
Self-Direction and Independent Living

Co-host: Welcome. Sometimes a helpful conversation moves away from a person's wishes before anyone notices. Let's work through a planning example and ask: how can we help someone understand a choice while keeping that choice in their hands?

Host: Consider Maya, who wants more consistency in the people supporting her at home. She is exploring a self-directed option because she hopes to hire someone she already trusts. Her situation gives us a way to think through a fair comparison of options.

Co-host: During a planning visit, Maya says that repeating her morning routine to unfamiliar workers wears her out. Her coordinator listens and then says that self-direction involves considerable paperwork. An agency arrangement, the coordinator explains, would probably be easier.

Host: I can understand that response. Staff see the forms, scheduling problems, and employer responsibilities. They may be trying to prevent disappointment. If someone is already stretched, shouldn't a coordinator explain that taking on additional responsibilities can be difficult?

Co-host: Absolutely. The difficulty belongs in the conversation. But easier for the coordinator, easier to administer, and easier for Maya are different questions. Her concern is unfamiliar people entering her home. A response about paperwork hasn't yet addressed what matters to her.

Host: So we haven't found bad intent. We've found an incomplete comparison. The coordinator has described one option mainly through its burden, while the other option's burden, the repeated introductions and disrupted routine, has almost disappeared from the discussion.

Co-host: A useful first question would be: what would you want to be different about your support? That gives Maya room to describe continuity, timing, privacy, or something we haven't anticipated, before we attach those wishes to a particular arrangement.

Host: In our example, Maya identifies two priorities. She wants fewer unfamiliar workers, and she wants more say over when support arrives. She is interested in hiring her neighbor, but that is a possible way to meet her priorities, not a promised outcome.

Co-host: Now we can explain the option more fairly. Minnesota describes consumer-directed community supports as offering greater choice and responsibility for eligible people. The choice can involve arranging supports, directing workers, and managing spending within an approved plan and the applicable program rules.

Host: And we should name the work plainly. Who develops the plan? Who recruits, trains, and schedules workers? What help is available with financial administration? Those questions matter because control over support should come with a usable explanation of what carrying that control involves.

Co-host: The coordinator doesn't need to settle every detail from memory. They can consult current program information and the people responsible for Maya's particular arrangement. The next conversation should distinguish what is confirmed, what needs checking, and what remains Maya's preference.

Host: That feels more honest than saying either, you can hire whoever you want, or, this is too complicated for you. Both statements close down questions that deserve attention. Neither tells Maya what support might make the option workable for her.

Co-host: Let's return to the coordinator. They try again: I understand that familiar support matters to you. We can compare what each arrangement would mean for your routine, the responsibilities you would take on, and the help you could use.

Host: Maya asks what happens if her preferred worker cannot come. That's a substantial concern. A warm conversation shouldn't skip it. A backup arrangement may matter as much as choosing the usual worker, especially when support is needed at a particular time.

Co-host: Exactly. The answer isn't to wave away the risk or use it to end the choice. Ask what coverage would be needed, what options are actually available, and who can help examine them. Then bring those findings back to Maya.

Host: We can hear the difference. In the first conversation, the concern was a reason to steer her away. In the second, the same concern becomes a planning question. The concern remains real, but it no longer silently decides the outcome.

Co-host: Maya also says that long forms are difficult to work through. That tells us something about the format and assistance she needs. It doesn't, by itself, tell us whether she can decide what kind of support fits her life.

Host: Would we offer a support planner at this point? Minnesota's information describes help with developing and monitoring a plan and with worker arrangements. That sounds relevant, provided we explain how that help fits the particular option and what it would involve.

Co-host: Yes. We should discuss available planning help and its cost or budget implications, where applicable. Assistance is part of the comparison, not an invisible favor we assume someone will supply. Maya should understand that part before weighing the alternatives.

Host: Her sister has offered to help with scheduling. The coordinator initially treats that as the solution. But we need to hear whether Maya wants that help, whether her sister can sustain it, and what happens if the arrangement becomes difficult.

Co-host: Let's put two workable possibilities beside each other. One involves exploring self-direction with verified planning and administrative support. The other involves discussing whether an agency arrangement could offer better continuity. We compare both against Maya's priorities, rather than assuming either is inherently better.

Host: For each possibility, we ask about familiar workers, scheduling, backup coverage, responsibilities, and available assistance. Some answers are known and some aren't. Naming those gaps helps Maya decide what she needs to learn before making a choice.

Co-host: The coordinator then invites Maya to explain the choices in her own words. That isn't a test of Maya. It is a check on the explanation. If something remains confusing, the responsibility is to find a clearer way to discuss it.

Host: What if Maya chooses the agency arrangement after all this? That is still a meaningful outcome. We haven't failed to promote self-direction. We've made the choice more informed and made her priorities more visible whichever arrangement she selects.

Co-host: And choosing to explore self-direction would not settle eligibility, approve a budget, or confirm a particular worker. Those questions follow their actual decision processes. Here, success means that Maya understands the possibilities and can influence what happens next.

Host: Maya asks to explore self-direction with the planning help they've discussed. The coordinator agrees to check the unanswered questions and return with a comparison she can use. Her sister joins the next conversation because Maya wants her there.

Co-host: The written record should preserve that meaning. Instead of a broad statement that Maya prefers the easier option, record her priorities, the possibilities discussed, the questions still open, and the next contact. Use her own words where they clarify the decision.

Host: That also helps the next colleague. They can see why continuity matters and what needs following up. Maya is less likely to have to rebuild the whole conversation just because a different person opens the file or answers the phone.

Co-host: For your next step, choose one conversation you expect to have. Prepare three questions: what matters most to this person, what responsibilities need explaining, and what assistance needs checking? Keep the questions close to the actual choice, rather than adding a long checklist.

Host: Then notice whether the person's answer changes your proposed next step. You might slow down, seek information, invite someone with permission, or compare a different option. Those are visible signs that listening is influencing the work rather than simply preceding it.

Co-host: The Self-Direction and Independent Living course includes a decision-support review you can use for that reflection. Its scenarios let you compare support with substitution, and consider how a person's wishes can remain visible when other people are concerned about practical risks.

Host: You can also use the Equity Analysis Toolkit to examine a repeated barrier across several decisions. For Maya, though, the immediate improvement is straightforward: explain the options fairly, make assistance visible, and let the next step reflect what she has told us.

pi-protecting-program-without-harm.transcript:
Protecting the Program Without Becoming the Harm

Co-host: Welcome. A program review can be necessary, and the way people hear about it can still cause avoidable harm. Let's work through a notice together. How could we explain the purpose of the review and give people information they can actually use?

Host: Our example involves a small provider serving people in a rural area. The provider has been selected for a routine, category-wide claims review. Some people using its services need information in another language. Nearby alternatives are limited, which makes uncertainty especially concerning.

Co-host: The team has prepared a draft communication for affected people. It says that the provider is under review and directs questions to a general office. It doesn't explain what kind of review this is or what the recipient needs to do.

Host: My first reaction is that a short notice avoids making promises before the review is finished. We shouldn't speculate about findings or create expectations the team cannot meet. Isn't cautious wording the sensible choice when some answers are still unknown?

Co-host: Caution is sensible. But silence can invite speculation too. Someone reading under review may wonder whether their next visit will happen, whether they have done something wrong, or whether they need a new provider. Those questions arise from the wording even when we don't mention them.

Host: So the issue isn't choosing between reassurance and accuracy. It's making the accurate information understandable, and being specific about what we haven't established. A vague letter can feel cautious to its writer while leaving its reader with the most alarming interpretation.

Co-host: Before rewriting, we need the facts behind this particular communication. What action has been authorized? What is its scope? Has any decision affecting services or payment been made? Who needs this information, and what response, if any, is actually requested?

Host: For this example, the reviewer confirms that this is a routine examination of claims, and no finding has yet been made. We can explain that confirmed purpose. We still can't predict the result or assume every recipient's circumstances are the same.

Co-host: We also ask who approved this audience and communication. A provider's records request and information for someone receiving services serve different purposes. Combining them into one generic message may leave both readers uncertain about which part applies to them.

Host: That distinction changes our draft. We aren't going to copy a document request into a notice for service recipients. We will explain the relevant action, any confirmed implications for the reader, and the contact who can answer questions about their situation.

Co-host: Imagine opening this letter while arranging support for tomorrow morning. The sentence about claims may be understandable, but the unanswered question is personal: what does this mean for the help I rely on? The letter needs to distinguish that question from the review itself.

Host: Could we simply add that services will continue? That would probably relieve anxiety. But we haven't checked whether that statement is authorized or accurate for everyone receiving the notice. A comforting sentence can become harmful when someone relies on information we haven't verified.

Co-host: Exactly. Confirm the current implications with the responsible team, and state only what that confirmation supports. If an individual situation needs discussion, make the route clear. We can be helpful without making a universal promise about payments, services, or the review's outcome.

Host: The same applies to timing. If the team has a supported estimate or an agreed update point, explain it accurately. If it doesn't, don't invent a deadline. Say how people can get an update and who is responsible for providing one.

Co-host: Now consider language. Sending an English notice and expecting a family member to explain it shifts important work onto the household. The team should use the appropriate language-access arrangements and make sure the question route is usable in the needed language too.

Host: Otherwise, we solve only half the problem. A translated letter that leads to an unanswered English-only phone message can still leave the person stranded. We should check the whole short journey, from receiving the notice to getting a relevant response.

Co-host: Let's draft the opening together. Start with the confirmed purpose: your provider has been selected for a routine claims review. Then explain what that means in ordinary language, using wording the reviewer has checked, rather than leaving the word review to carry every implication.

Host: Next, separate what we know from what remains open. We can explain that the review has not reached a finding. We can add verified information about current arrangements. We should also clearly identify any action the recipient is actually being asked to take.

Co-host: Then give a contact that fits the question. A named role may be more sustainable than an individual name if coverage changes. What matters is that someone receives the question, understands the notice, and knows how to connect it with the responsible colleague.

Host: There is a real workload tradeoff here. A clearer notice may prompt questions the old notice suppressed. We shouldn't call that failure automatically. Those questions may reveal uncertainty that already existed, while giving the team a chance to address it before it spreads.

Co-host: But we shouldn't create a contact route without preparing it either. Before sending, check who will respond, what they can explain, and where questions outside their role go. A promising sentence at the bottom of the page needs an actual person or team behind it.

Host: The reviewer checks that the revised wording preserves the facts. A communication colleague checks whether readers can find the purpose and next step. Language and accessibility support are arranged for the intended recipients. Each contribution improves a particular part of the same message.

Co-host: After those checks, the team sends the revised notice. Questions still arrive. One person asks whether they need to send records. Another wants help understanding their own situation. The team can use those questions to see where the explanation still needs work.

Host: The team records the kinds of questions without placing unnecessary personal details in a shared learning note. They clarify the confusing sentence for the next communication and check whether the contact route is resolving questions or simply passing people between offices.

Co-host: We can't conclude that fewer calls prove better understanding. People may stop calling because they are satisfied, because the explanation worked, or because they couldn't reach anyone. Ask about understanding and the usefulness of the response alongside the number of contacts.

Host: And don't treat one person's account as everyone's experience. A few conversations can reveal problems worth investigating, but they don't measure the whole population. They help us ask a better question about who is being reached and whose questions remain unanswered.

Co-host: This is where the Equity Analysis Toolkit can strengthen ordinary work. Define the actual decision, identify affected people, consider evidence and missing perspectives, compare communication options, and explain what you will check afterward. The analysis should change something identifiable in the notice or its support.

Host: In this case, it changed the distinction between review and finding, the explanation relevant to recipients, the language arrangements, and the next contact. We haven't weakened oversight. We've reduced avoidable uncertainty that was never necessary to accomplish the review.

Co-host: For your own work, choose one upcoming communication. Read it as someone whose daily arrangements might be affected. Can you find what is happening, what it means for you, what you need to do, and where a real question would receive an answer?

Host: The Protecting the Program Without Becoming the Harm course includes notice comparisons and toolkit practice for that task. Start with one sentence or one unanswered question. A specific, verified improvement can protect both the integrity of the program and the people who depend on it.

cn-building-a-navigator-role.transcript:
A Role, Not a Favor

Kelly: A manager gets funding for one navigator and wants them to help any family, in any language, at any step. What's the problem?

John: One person can't do that. They'd be spread so thin you'd never see a difference.

Kelly: And the evidence points the other way. Navigation tends to help most when it's tied to a specific step. A 2021 trial of family navigation for autism found more families got a diagnostic answer within a year, though results varied by clinic. So start by finding where people get lost in your own process, and focus there.

John: Then you write the job.

Kelly: Write the duties, and write what the role is not. The C3 Project's list of community health worker roles is a good menu: cultural mediation, system navigation, advocacy, outreach. And the not list matters just as much. Not an interpreter unless they're qualified and hired for it. Not a decision maker. Not overflow case management.

John: Here's the one I see. No budget, so we ask our bilingual staff to just come along on a few visits.

Kelly: That's navigation without the job. It's unpaid, nobody counts it, and it can leave that person caught between their community and their work. Name it, count it, and either make it part of a recognized role or move it to one.

John: Should the navigator work for the agency, or for a community organization?

Kelly: Both can work. Inside, you get easier access to systems. Through a community partner, you often get deeper trust. M Health Fairview's cultural brokers, for example, spend most of their time at trusted community organizations.

John: And once they're hired?

Kelly: Supervise both sides of the work. Keep navigators out of enforcement and bad-news roles, so they keep the community's trust. And plan caseloads with secondary traumatic stress in mind. Hearing hard stories every day has a cost.

John: A clear purpose, a written scope, fair pay and real support. A role, not a favor.

cn-culture-in-informed-choice.transcript:
Cultural Needs: None?

Kelly: I want to start with a field on a form. Cultural needs. And the answer, again and again, is none identified.

John: Honestly, that question feels awkward to ask. People usually mention what matters to them.

Kelly: Usually they don't, at least not to someone from an agency. And Minnesota law treats it as part of the process. For people using waiver services, informed decision making includes identification of the person's cultural needs and access to culturally responsive services and providers.

John: So how do you ask without it being awkward or stereotyping?

Kelly: Open questions about what matters. What's important to you in how people help you at home? Anything about your faith, food or routines helpers should know? Who do you want with you when decisions are made? Which language are you most comfortable in?

John: And not, people from that community usually prefer this.

Kelly: Exactly. Background can suggest a question. It never answers it.

John: Say the person wants helpers who speak their language, and there aren't any in the county.

Kelly: Widen the search. Ask navigators and community organizations what they know. Ask providers specific questions about what they could adapt. Bring the options back and let the person choose. And record honestly what you looked for and didn't find.

John: Why record the gap?

Kelly: Because a hidden gap never gets fixed. One record is a person's story. A pattern of the same gap is something the program can act on.

John: And in the plan itself?

Kelly: Be specific, in the person's words. Prefers family tells a new helper almost nothing. Wants their sister present for decisions, prefers a female helper for bathing, tells them what to do. And ask again when life changes.

cn-navigating-disability-services-with-a.transcript:
A Map, One Step at a Time

Kelly: A parent hands a navigator a stack of papers and says, I don't know what any of this is. Where do you start?

John: Not with all of it, I hope.

Kelly: Right. Find the one paper that matters now, explain it and write down the next step. The whole path has five parts: first contact, assessment, planning and choice, services starting, and renewals and changes. But a family only needs the next step today.

John: Who does the assessment in Minnesota?

Kelly: Lead agencies: counties, tribal nations and managed care organizations, using the state's MnCHOICES system and certified assessors. A navigator doesn't assess. A navigator helps the family get ready.

John: Some families want to show they're doing fine, so nobody thinks they can't cope.

Kelly: That's very human. The navigator can explain that the assessment is how the agency learns what help might make life easier, and talk through a real week with them, hard nights included. Then the family decides what to share, in their own words. Preparing, never scripting.

John: Then they get a list of providers and a deadline.

Kelly: And this is where the law helps. For people on waivers, Minnesota's informed decision-making process includes things like all available options, cultural needs, visits or hands-on experiences, talking with peers and enough time to decide. A family who knows they can ask for a visit is in a much stronger position.

John: And once services are approved, it's done?

Kelly: Not quite. That's when things quietly stall. Help the family know what should happen next, follow up with the case manager when they agree, read every letter together for dates and appeal rights, and keep a simple record.

John: And free help along the way?

Kelly: Disability Hub MN is a free statewide resource. For health coverage, MNsure navigators help for free too. A navigator doesn't have to know everything. They have to know where to go.

cn-navigators-and-system-change.transcript:
The Letter Five Families Misread

Kelly: A navigator tells a program manager that five families this month misread the same renewal letter and thought their services were ending.

John: And the easy answer is, that letter uses required wording.

Kelly: Some of it might. But the explanation around it, the headings, a plain summary at the top, the translations, those usually can change. And if the navigator hears, nothing we can do, they'll stop reporting. Feeding back is part of a navigator's job. Listening is part of ours.

John: So we rewrite every letter the program sends?

Kelly: Start smaller. The Institute for Healthcare Improvement describes the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle: plan a test, try it, study what happened and decide what to change. Try the new renewal letter with ten families before ten thousand. Navigators can tell you quickly whether people understood it.

John: Then we can announce that the new letter cut missed renewals by half.

Kelly: Careful there. Measure the step you meant to change, and say what you compared with and what else changed at the same time. There's a real difference between strong evidence and program-reported results.

John: What's an example?

Kelly: The 2021 autism family navigation trial assigned families by chance, so it's strong evidence. A newspaper reported that 96 percent of 499 families served by Sacramento County's Cultural Broker program had emergency referrals closed without court involvement. That figure came from the program. Useful, but there's no comparison group, so it can't show how much the brokers caused.

John: And when the fix works?

Kelly: Give credit to the navigator who spotted it and the organization they work for. Tell them what changed, and what couldn't. That's what keeps the next report coming.

John: Listen, test small, measure honestly and share the credit.

cn-sustaining-the-navigator.transcript:
Carrying It

Kelly: Navigators hear hard stories all day, often from their own community. That has a name: secondary traumatic stress. The National Child Traumatic Stress Network describes it as distress that comes from hearing about someone else's trauma.

John: What does it look like?

Kelly: Exhaustion, trouble sleeping, hopelessness, getting cynical, avoiding the people you serve. And the risk goes up with things that fit this work: heavy caseloads, isolation, a lot of empathy and feeling unprepared.

John: And then there's the phone. Community members calling at night, on weekends, at the grocery store.

Kelly: Boundary strain. Saying no can feel like letting your own people down. But a kind boundary protects the relationship. Something like, I want to help with this. I'm off now, so let's talk tomorrow at nine. If it's an emergency, call this number.

John: Is this mostly on the navigator, then? Self-care?

Kelly: Most of it is on the organization. The fact sheet names balanced caseloads, flexible scheduling, ongoing training and supervision. Nobody can self-care their way out of a caseload that doubled.

John: So if I supervise a navigator who's gone quiet and is missing follow-ups?

Kelly: Meet privately, say what you've noticed without labeling, ask how they're carrying it and look at the caseload together. And make sure they know about confidential help, like the Employee Assistance Program.

John: Notice early, share the load and set boundaries kindly. That's how the work lasts.

cn-what-a-navigator-does.transcript:
Who Helps at Home?

Kelly: Picture an assessment. The assessor asks who helps the person at home, and the person's mother says, family takes care of family. What gets written down?

John: Probably something like, daily help covered by family. It sounds clear. It sounds like a strong family.

Kelly: And it might be. But in this case the mother works nights. The family didn't want to look like they couldn't cope in front of someone from the county. So the clear answer was true and incomplete at the same time.

John: And if nobody catches that, the plan has a hole in it on exactly the nights that matter.

Kelly: That's where a cultural navigator can help. A navigator is a trusted go-between, often someone from the person's community, who helps a family and a system understand each other. In this case the navigator simply asked the mother whether she wanted to mention her schedule.

John: So the navigator didn't answer for the family.

Kelly: No, and that matters. The family still speaks for itself. The navigator explains context, goes along to meetings, connects people to resources, follows up, and tells the agency where a process keeps tripping people up.

John: Is there evidence this works, or is it just a nice idea?

Kelly: There's some good evidence when navigation is tied to a specific step. A 2021 randomized trial of family navigation for young children who screened positive for autism found that more families got a diagnostic answer within a year. The difference was largest for Hispanic families. The authors also found results varied by clinic, so it's promising, not magic.

John: Here's a question I hear a lot. If the navigator speaks the family's language, can we skip the interpreter?

Kelly: Book both. The interpreter carries the words accurately in both directions. The navigator helps the family make sense of the process. If the navigator is interpreting, nobody is doing the navigating.

John: And the version where we ask the bilingual coworker to just come along on a few visits?

Kelly: That's navigation work without the job. It adds work nobody counts, and it can leave that coworker caught between their community and their role. If the need is real, treat it as real work, and tell someone who can fix the pattern.

John: So for someone listening who isn't a navigator, what's the one thing to do?

Kelly: When an answer could mean more than one thing, check before you write it down. Ask about specific hours and tasks. And if a navigator might help, ask the person whether they'd like one. It's their choice, and what they share is their choice too.

John: Check the answer, offer the choice, and give everyone a clear role. I can do that on Monday.

cn-working-alongside-a-navigator.transcript:
Three People, One Meeting

Kelly: Here's a common call. A navigator rings a case manager before a planning meeting and says, send me everything in the file so I can be ready. What do you do?

John: My instinct is to send it. The family asked for the navigator, so they must be fine with it.

Kelly: Asking for a navigator isn't the same as agreeing to share everything. In Minnesota, releasing someone's private data to another person takes their informed consent, which is written permission. So check the release first, and then share what the meeting needs, not the whole file.

John: What does the meeting usually need?

Kelly: What the meeting is for, what decisions might come up, any deadlines, who's interpreting and what the person wants help with. And five minutes agreeing on roles. Who explains, who interprets, who supports the person and who decides.

John: Then the meeting starts, and I ask the person about their day, and the navigator answers for them. It's helpful. It's also not the person.

Kelly: Thank the navigator and turn back to the person. Something like, that helps me understand, I'd like to hear from you too. A good navigator welcomes that. Their job is to help the person speak, not to speak for them.

John: And at the end?

Kelly: Ask the person to tell you in their own words what happens next. If it's not what you expected, the gap is in your explanation, not in them.

John: What about when the navigator pushes back? Says the provider list leaves out options that fit the family.

Kelly: That's often a sign the role is working. Brokers and navigators advocate. Ask what they're seeing, separate what the rules require from what's just habit and check whether there are options you didn't know about. Talk privately first, unless the choice is the family's. Then the family belongs in the conversation.

John: And afterward I send the family a plain-language note of what happens next.

Kelly: And with their agreement, keep the navigator informed. Families often call the navigator first. If the navigator knows the request was approved, they can share good news instead of guessing.

John: Consent first, clear roles, the person at the center, and close the loop. I can do that.

cw-everyday-norms.transcript:
The Typo That Changed a Team

Kelly: Picture a newer colleague three months into the job. They send a client letter with one typo. Within an hour it comes up in a team chat, in a reply-all and in a one-on-one. Nobody is unkind. So what did that colleague just learn?

John: That a typo is a big deal here. Probably bigger than the policy says. And that the safest move is to have three people check every routine letter from now on.

Kelly: Right. Nobody wrote that rule down. The team taught it in an afternoon. That is what culture is: the shared habits and assumptions that tell people what really matters, mostly without words.

John: But accuracy matters. A wrong address on a notice can mean someone misses an appointment. I don't want us to get casual about that.

Kelly: Neither do I. The question isn't whether to keep a high standard. It's whether the response matches the stakes. A clear check for things that can hurt someone is a standard. Treating every small slip as a crisis is a habit, and it has costs.

John: Like the three reviewers for a routine letter. That's time those reviewers aren't spending with families.

Kelly: And something quieter. When mistakes feel dangerous, people stop mentioning them. Research on team learning has found that stronger teams sometimes report more errors, not fewer, because people feel safe enough to say so.

John: So the number of mistakes you hear about isn't the same as the number that happen.

Kelly: Exactly. Silence can look like quality from the outside.

John: Say a notice did go out with the wrong office address, and a client traveled to the old location. What does a good response sound like?

Kelly: Start with the person affected: fix it for them first. Then ask what about the process let it happen, before asking who. Was the address stored in three places? Did the template pull an old value?

John: And the person who sent it is in the room, probably feeling awful.

Kelly: Which is why the supervisor goes first if they can. Something like, here's what happened, here's what we've already fixed for the client, and here's the part of our process I want us to look at together.

John: Here's the harder one for me. What if the mistake is the supervisor's? A wrong deadline in the team update, and you're the newest person there.

Kelly: Keep it short, private and about the work. I think the report deadline in the update might be the 15th, not the 20th. Want me to check? That's it. No apology tour.

John: And if the supervisor thanks them for it, in front of the team, the next person speaks up faster.

Kelly: That's how a norm shifts. Not with a poster. With what happens the next time someone says, I think we got this wrong.

John: In the course, you'll practice telling standards from habits, and responding to mistakes in a way that keeps people talking.

cw-learning-organization.transcript:
When Leaders Hear "Resistance"

Kelly: Three months after a new intake process launched, a manager in the leadership meeting says frontline staff are resisting it. Two other supervisors say the same thing.

John: As a director, I'd hear that as a change management problem. More training, more communication.

Kelly: Maybe. But resistance is often information arriving in a form leaders don't like. What are staff seeing that we aren't? The research on learning organizations says culture is built by systems: how we gather information, how we review, how we decide.

John: Then a case manager asks for five minutes and says the new form is causing families to give up partway through. And I championed that form.

Kelly: That's the moment that decides whether the next person comes to you. What's your first sentence?

John: Honestly? Probably a defense of why we built it.

Kelly: Most of us would. Try, thank you for bringing this to me directly. Show me where families stop. Then the follow-up matters even more: tell them what you did with it.

John: Because the whole floor will know how that conversation went by lunch.

Kelly: Now a blameless review of a missed deadline. Partway through, a supervisor starts to say which case manager made the error.

John: And the facilitator has to step in.

Kelly: Kindly and quickly. Something like, let's stay with how the process worked, and come back to individual follow-up separately. The point of the review is to find what the system made easy to get wrong.

John: Which is why the facilitator shouldn't be the person whose decision is under review.

Kelly: Last one. The program manager has a draft policy ready. It changes how families submit paperwork. The county partner and the counties haven't seen it.

John: Sending it as final saves weeks.

Kelly: It might. But the people closest to families will find the problems eventually. The only question is whether they find them before launch or after. Share it as a draft, say what can still change, and set a date.

John: So a learning organization isn't a slogan. It's a set of routines leaders design and protect.

Kelly: That's what this course is for: building those routines in your own division.

cw-pace-pressure-decisions.transcript:
Is It Really Due Today?

John: Four in the afternoon. A supervisor gets a request: send updated guidance to every case manager by end of day. The guidance changes how a form is filled out, and the supervisor hasn't read it closely.

Kelly: First question: who set the end of day, and what happens if it goes out tomorrow morning instead?

John: Sometimes the answer is, a law says so. Often it's, someone just said by end of day.

Kelly: And that difference matters. Research on decisions under time pressure finds people shift to shortcuts. They look at less information and lean on what's quick. Fine for low stakes. Risky for guidance a whole division will follow.

Kelly: Here's another. The monthly report shows four hundred cases closed, a record. The program manager is preparing remarks.

John: Celebrate it, surely. People worked hard.

Kelly: Celebrate the effort, yes. But ask what four hundred closures means for people. How many closed because services started, and how many because a form wasn't returned?

John: Ah. A closed case isn't the same as a family that got help.

Kelly: Output is what we produce. Outcomes are what changes for people. Under pressure, output is easier to count, so it quietly becomes the goal.

John: So what do you actually do in the moment? End of day, a case manager is about to close a case because a form never came back.

Kelly: A short pause routine. Three questions: who does this affect, what would I need to know to be confident, and is anything about this situation unusual?

John: And in this case a colleague mentions the household's preferred language isn't English, and the reminder went out in English only.

Kelly: Then the pause just did its job. The right next step is a reminder they can read, not a closure.

John: But some deadlines can't move. A new eligibility process launches on a date set by law, and notices in Somali and Hmong won't be ready for two more weeks.

Kelly: Then you protect quality another way. A quick premortem helps: imagine it's a month after launch and it went badly for families who read Somali or Hmong. What happened?

John: They never heard about the change. Or they heard and didn't know what to do.

Kelly: So you plan for that now: community partners, interpreters on the phone line, extra time to respond. The date holds. The harm doesn't have to.

John: That's the whole course: tell a true deadline from a habit, and protect the decisions that matter most.

cw-sustainable-pace.transcript:
Running on Empty, Quietly

Kelly: Here's someone a lot of us know. A case manager, two years with a full caseload, and really good at it. Lately they answer email at ten at night, skip lunch and feel flat even after a good outcome for a family.

John: Nothing's on fire. The work is getting done. So is there actually a problem?

Kelly: That's the trap. The early signs are quiet. Feeling flat after a win is one of them. The World Health Organization describes burnout as a result of workplace stress that hasn't been managed: exhaustion, growing distance from the work and feeling less effective.

John: So it's about the conditions at work, not a personal failing.

Kelly: Right. And that matters, because it means some of the fixes are things a team can change together.

John: Okay, practical moment. It's 9:45 at night. A colleague emails a non-urgent question about next week's schedule. I'm going to answer it. It takes thirty seconds.

Kelly: It does. And it also tells your colleague that late-night answers are normal here. Next week, they'll feel they should answer at ten, too.

John: Huh. So the thirty seconds isn't really the cost.

Kelly: No. One small protection is to schedule the reply for the morning, or simply answer it at nine. The question still gets answered. The norm doesn't spread.

John: What about when it's more than email? Caseload up by a third since spring, two reports late, and I haven't said anything to my supervisor.

Kelly: That's the moment to raise it, while it's two reports and not ten. Bring facts and a question: here's what's changed, here's what's slipping, which of these should I put first?

John: That's much easier to say than, I'm not coping.

Kelly: And it's more useful to a supervisor. They can actually decide something.

John: Last one. A colleague has seemed withdrawn for a few weeks and left early twice without saying goodbye. I don't want to pry.

Kelly: You don't have to diagnose anything. A private, simple check-in works: I've noticed you seem a bit quieter lately. How are you doing? Then listen, and let them decide how much to share.

John: And if they're really struggling?

Kelly: Know where support lives. Minnesota's state Employee Assistance Program is free, voluntary and confidential, for state employees and the people they live with. And if someone may be in crisis, the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline answers by call, text or chat, any time.

John: So the course isn't about fixing anyone. It's about noticing early, and knowing the next step.

cw-trauma-informed-teams.transcript:
A Lobby Like a Police Station

John: A county partner tells a program manager that families describe the lobby as like a police station. The security check is required, and several families have left before their interviews.

Kelly: So the check stays. The question is everything around it. SAMHSA's trauma-informed approach has six principles: safety, trustworthiness and transparency, peer support, collaboration, empowerment and choice, and attention to cultural, historical and gender issues.

John: Run the lobby through those, and you get practical ideas. A sign that explains why the check exists. A greeting before the screening, not after. A place to wait that doesn't feel like a holding area.

Kelly: None of that weakens security. It just stops security from being the first and only message.

Kelly: Here's the appointment letter a case manager is asked to revise. You must appear at the office on the date below. Failure to appear will result in case closure.

John: Accurate. And frightening, if you've had bad experiences with systems.

Kelly: Keep the facts and change the stance. Lead with what the appointment is for, offer a way to reschedule and say who to call. The consequence can still be there, stated plainly, near the end.

John: Now the staff side. A team handled a child fatality review this week. Several people were closely involved. The program manager wants to respond.

Kelly: Secondary traumatic stress is real. The National Child Traumatic Stress Network describes it as the emotional duress that results when a person hears about the firsthand trauma experiences of another.

John: So a cheerful team lunch isn't the answer.

Kelly: Not on its own. Acknowledge what happened, offer some flexibility with the next few days, and remind people about the Employee Assistance Program, which is confidential. Then check in again next week, not just once.

John: Last one is mine to lead. A leadership meeting will cover a staff assault from last month. Some people in the room were there when it happened.

Kelly: Tell people beforehand what will be discussed, so nobody is surprised. Say at the start that stepping out is fine. Keep the focus on what the division is changing, not on reliving the details.

John: Choice and transparency again.

Kelly: Exactly. The six principles work for staff as much as for families. That's the heart of this course.

cw-workload-burnout.transcript:
The Person Who Always Says Yes

John: A team lost two positions last year, and the work stayed the same. Two people are on leave. Then a difficult new case comes in, the kind one case manager always handles well.

Kelly: And that case manager is already covering more than anyone. So it goes to them. Again.

John: It's efficient, though.

Kelly: Today. The burnout research points to six areas of work life that matter: workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values. Giving the hard case to the same person every time touches at least three of them.

John: So the supervisor raises it in a one-on-one, and the case manager says, I'm fine, it's just a busy season.

Kelly: But the supervisor has seen late-night emails for most of the month. The mistake would be to argue about whether they're fine.

John: Because they'll just dig in.

Kelly: Right. Name what you've noticed, without judgment, and make it about the work. I've seen a lot of late emails this month. That tells me the load isn't working. What's one thing I could take off or move?

John: So the supervisor owns the problem, instead of asking the person to admit they're struggling.

Kelly: Exactly. Workload is a design problem. The supervisor has the levers.

John: Here's where I get nervous. A supervisor proposes a shared weekly view of caseloads. As a newer person, I'd worry it'll be used to judge whoever is slower.

Kelly: That worry is the whole design question. Say clearly what the view is for: spotting when one person is overloaded and moving work. Not ranking anyone. Agree it as a team, and review it after a month.

John: And notice who doesn't speak. If someone with years on the team stays silent, that's worth a private follow-up.

Kelly: Last piece. The program manager asks the supervisor how the team is doing. Caseloads up thirty percent, two people on leave, two reports late.

John: The instinct is to say, we're managing.

Kelly: And then nothing changes above you. Give the facts plainly, say what's at risk, and bring a choice: here's what we can keep on time, here's what will slip, which would you protect?

John: That's not complaining. That's giving your manager something to decide.

Kelly: And it protects your team. That's what this course practices: seeing the drivers, holding the conversation, and changing how the work is shared.
